title: Duke's stage presentation and conducting
summary: Duke could not remember names when introducing singers early on and seldom conducted before extended works.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Cootie, I'd like to talk to you. You remember this and I remember this, but a whole lot of people don't. Remember how, the Ellington -- the famous Ellington style, you know, the personality and approach and everything on stage that everybody knows so well. I remember full well when he didn't have any of it. And I guess you do too. Do you remember how he used to come out on stage and he never could remember the name of the person he was going to introduce?
(Laughter)
That's right. But, I don't know, years go by, you know, you acquire all those things.
Yeah. But don't you remember, he'd give the singer the big buildup. The beautiful, the gorgeous and everything, and then he couldn't put his tongue on the name, remember?
Yeah.
And he'd be turning around and asking -- somebody was supposed to be telling him from behind -- Johnny
Hodges or --
Sonny would help him.

Or Sonny. Sonny would help. Well, I mean, even for conducting the band, I mean, don't you remember, [he used not] you started to conduct the band so much. He mostly gave the beat and went to the piano. Am I right or am I wrong on that? Do you think he always did conduct? Quite a bit?
No, he never did conduct the band, unless it was a special number.
Yeah.
No, he never did conduct the band. He started the band off on the piano, then that was it. No, he never did conduct the band.
Well, but in later years, when he had the -- well, for instance, when he got the extended works and so on.
Yeah.
Then he began to conduct.
Yeah. He had to conduct then.
Yeah. He had to conduct, didn't he?
Yeah.
And he took a fancy to it, too, because he -- you know, he could -- I mean he looked very good from behind, you know. It was a good selling point, the way he conducted in the end, don't you think?
Yeah.
But in the beginning I think he felt a little ill at ease, didn't he?
Well, he did. Which he used to have a saying that he's no good without the band.
Yeah. Yeah.
And I used to say, 'Well, the band is no good without you.'
(Laughter)
Which was a true saying.
